title: Weaver, shoemaker, barber, king
hook: the Bhagats' trades read like a street; that's the point

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing edited out: the Gurus kept the Bhagats' words whole and answered beside them. Your line was answer, don't erase. Did you repeat someone's words fairly before replying? Day seven hundred ninety-six.

A clatter from a loom in a doorway. Next door, someone bent over a shoe, stitching leather. Further on, a barber with a razor and a customer half-shaved. A farmer coming in from the fields with mud on his feet. And at the end of the road, a palace. Walk the names of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib and that's the street you're walking down: weaver, shoemaker, barber, king.
screen: `A LOOM IN A DOORWAY.` → `LEATHER, A RAZOR, A MUDDY FARMER.` → `A PALACE AT THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Some of these trades come from the Bhagats' own mouths. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his hymns, and works the loom into his songs. Namdev says he was born in the house of a calico printer. Ravidas says his family carried the dead cattle, work the caste order of his day looked down on. Others come from tradition: Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne. Put them side by side and they don't read like a list of holy men from one class. They read like a street. That's the point. Ravidas's own hymns show a town that ranked people by birth, where a leather-worker's touch was counted as polluting. The Granth answers by putting the weaver's song, the leather worker's song and the king's song on the same pages, in the same raags, under the same honor. The barber's hymn is sung with the same reverence as the king's. Guru Nanak says it in his own words in Raag Asa, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. So this isn't decoration. The mix of trades is the teaching, made visible. You can't hold the Guru Granth Sahib in your hands and keep the street out of it. And that runs both ways. The king isn't shut out either. Pipa's place there is as a devotee, beside the others, not above them.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS: LOOM, PRINT, CATTLE.` · `IN TRADITION: BARBER, FARMER, KING.` · `DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · `THE MIX IS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE STREET.`

segments.voice: For the practice, greet three different workers. In the sit, walk your own street the way we walked the Bhagats'. Whoever drives the bus, stacks the shelves, cuts hair, answers the phone, runs the office. Picture their faces as clearly as you can. Then choose three you'll actually see today, and decide to greet each one properly: eyes up, a real hello, a name if you can learn it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Weaver. Kabir's own word for himself, at the head of a street of Bhagats: weaver, printer, leather worker, barber, farmer, king.
Your line: the whole street. Today, greet three people doing three different jobs, and look each of them in the eye. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs point to the Bhagats' different trades and castes as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's teaching that birth sets no limit on devotion, and the langar, where all sit together, puts the same teaching into practice.

fork.setup: you're gathering holy songs, and the best ones come from a weaver, a leather worker and a barber. birth is supposed to shut them out. what do you do?
options: keep only the songs by the high-born.
keep the songs but hide who wrote them.
keep them, under their own names, beside everyone else's.
fork.reveal: the Granth keeps their songs under their own names, in the same raags and with the same honor; the mix is the teaching.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a devotee; the Granth's name for these poets from every trade.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of saints' jobs.
what it means: weaver, printer, leather worker, barber, farmer and king sit on the same pages; birth doesn't decide who reaches God.
what a scholar hears: some trades come from the Bhagats' own verses (Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas), others from tradition (Sain, Dhanna, Pipa); the Granth's mix is itself a statement.

notes: Kabir calling himself a weaver (julaha) and Namdev saying he was born in a calico printer's (chhipa) house: from their hymns; a Keeper may wish to add Ang references.

Ravidas, 'my family carried the dead cattle' (meri jaat kutband dhaalaa dhor dhovantaa): cited as Malar, Ang 1293; confirm Ang. 'Work the caste order of his day looked down on' reflects the caste order of the time; confirm wording.
Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne: attributed to tradition.
'The Gurus' own hymns say what counts before God is not caste but devotion and deeds': general; a Keeper may wish to cite a line.

Editor pass: replaced the unsourced historical sweep ('birth decided who could approach God, read the texts, stand near the temple') with what Ravidas's cited hymns show, replaced the general 'the Gurus' hymns say' with a paraphrase of Guru Nanak's Asa line (jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee, aagai jaat na he, Ang 349: confirm Ang) and added it to sources; reworked the practice so it doesn't repeat day 778's unseen-worker angle; varied the hook ending and practice opener.

Audit (2026-10-01): checked the trades (Kabir julaha, Namdev chhipa at Asa Ang 485, Ravidas at Malar Ang 1293), the polluting-touch picture (Ravidas, Maru Ang 1106, day 777) and Asa Ang 349. No change.
